title: What is the difference between a topic, a partition, and an offset in Kafka?
shortTitle: Topic, partition, and offset in Kafka

s1_definition.profdef: In Kafka, a topic is a named, logical category of events, like a folder for a particular kind of record. Each topic is physically split into one or more partitions, which are ordered, append-only, immutable logs stored on brokers; partitions are the unit of parallelism and ordering. An offset is a monotonically increasing integer that uniquely identifies the position of a record within a specific partition. A record is therefore located by the triple topic, partition, and offset, and consumers track their progress by committing offsets.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India's record-keeping. A topic is like a labeled filing cabinet called "transfers" — it holds all transfer records. A partition is like one drawer inside that cabinet; the cabinet has several drawers so many clerks can work in parallel. An offset is like the sequential page number written on each sheet in a drawer — page 0, page 1, page 2, and so on. To find any single record you say the cabinet name (topic), the drawer number (partition), and the page number (offset).
s1_definition.oneliner: A topic is the category, a partition is one ordered log within that category, and an offset is the exact position of a record inside that partition.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Kafka, a topic is a named, logical category of events, like a folder for a particular kind of record. Each topic is physically split into one or more partitions, which are ordered, append-only, immutable logs stored on brokers; partitions are the unit of parallelism and ordering. An offset is a monotonically increasing integer that uniquely identifies the position of a record within a specific partition. A record is therefore located by the triple topic, partition, and offset, and consumers track their progress by committing offsets.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India's record-keeping. A topic is like a labeled filing cabinet called "transfers" — it holds all transfer records. A partition is like one drawer inside that cabinet; the cabinet has several drawers so many clerks can work in parallel. An offset is like the sequential page number written on each sheet in a drawer — page 0, page 1, page 2, and so on. To find any single record you say the cabinet name (topic), the drawer number (partition), and the page number (offset).

**One line to remember:** A topic is the category, a partition is one ordered log within that category, and an offset is the exact position of a record inside that partition.

sections.s2_technical:
A topic is purely a logical name; it does not store anything by itself. When you create a topic you specify how many partitions it has, because partitions are where the real data lives. In a banking system you might have topics named `transfers`, `transactions`, and `trade.settled`, each representing a distinct event category.

A partition is an ordered, append-only sequence of records. New records are always appended to the end, and records are never modified once written. Kafka guarantees ordering only within a single partition, not across partitions. Each partition is stored as a set of segment files on a broker's disk, and it can be replicated to other brokers for fault tolerance. The number of partitions determines the maximum parallelism of a consumer group, because one partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in a group at a time.

The record's placement in a partition is decided by its key. If you produce with a key, Kafka hashes the key and uses the hash to pick the partition, so the same key always lands in the same partition. For example, keying by account id with `kafkaTemplate.send("transfers", "SAV2001", transferJson)` ensures all of Rajesh's transfers go to the same partition and stay ordered relative to one another. If you produce without a key, Kafka distributes records across partitions in a balanced way.

An offset is a 64-bit integer assigned by the broker when a record is appended. Offsets start at 0 and increase by one for each new record in that partition. Offsets are per-partition, so partition 0 and partition 1 each have their own offset 0. A consumer reads records in offset order within a partition and periodically commits the offset of the last processed record. The committed offset is stored in an internal Kafka topic called `__consumer_offsets`. When a consumer restarts, it resumes from the last committed offset, which is how Kafka remembers progress. A consumer can also seek to an older offset to replay data: `consumer.seek(partition, 100)` rewinds to offset 100.

The senior-level nuance is that offsets are the key to Kafka's replay capability and its delivery guarantees. Committing the offset after processing gives at-least-once delivery, while committing before processing gives at-most-once. Because offsets are durable and per-partition, Kafka can let a brand new consumer group read the entire history of a topic from offset 0 while another group reads only new records from the latest offset — both at the same time without interference.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is building its transfer event stream, and the team must understand exactly how a transfer record is stored and found.

Problem 1 — The bank processes thousands of transfers per second and needs many workers to handle them in parallel, but the events for one account must stay in order. This is exactly why we split the `transfers` topic into several partitions and key each event by account id — many drawers for parallelism, but one account's events always in the same drawer in order.

Problem 2 — If a consumer crashes mid-way, it must resume exactly where it left off, not reprocess everything and not skip anything. This is exactly what offsets solve — the consumer remembers the last offset it committed and resumes from there.

Problem 3 — The fraud team wants to replay the last few events to re-check an account after a model update. This is exactly the seek-to-offset capability — rewind the partition to an earlier offset and read again.

The mini-project is a small in-memory Kafka model. We build a `TransferRecord` domain object, a `Partition` class that is an append-only list tracking offsets, a `Topic` class that holds several partitions and routes a record to a partition by hashing its key, and a `TransferConsumer` that reads from a partition starting at a committed offset and can seek backward. The demo produces several transfers for Rajesh and Priya, shows which partition and offset each landed at, consumes them, and then replays from an earlier offset.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four transfer records: TXF-1, TXF-2, TXF-4 keyed by SAV2001 and TXF-3 keyed by CUR3001.

Step 1 — The topic `transfers` is created with 3 partitions. No data exists yet; each partition's end offset is 0.

Step 2 — TXF-1 is produced with key SAV2001. The topic hashes SAV2001 to pick a partition, say partition 2, and appends the record. The broker assigns offset 0 in that partition and returns it.

Step 3 — TXF-2 is produced with the same key SAV2001. It hashes to the same partition 2 and is appended at offset 1. Because the key is identical, Rajesh's second transfer is guaranteed to sit right after his first in the same ordered log.

Step 4 — TXF-3 is produced with key CUR3001. It hashes to a different partition, say partition 0, and gets offset 0 there. Priya's events are isolated in their own partition with their own offset sequence.

Step 5 — TXF-4 with key SAV2001 lands in partition 2 at offset 2. Rajesh now has offsets 0, 1, 2 in order.

Step 6 — The consumer reads Rajesh's partition from offset 0 and processes TXF-1, TXF-2, TXF-4 in exact order. Later the fraud team seeks to offset 1 and replays TXF-2 and TXF-4, demonstrating that offsets make replay possible without touching the other partition.

```
  │ + produce(key, record): void  │
  │ + partition(id): Partition    │

                 │ 1..*
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │          Partition            │
  │ - id: int                     │
  │ - log: List<TransferRecord>   │  index == offset
  │ ──────────────────────────────│
  │ + append(record): int  (offset)│
  │ + at(offset): TransferRecord  │
  │ + endOffset(): long           │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │       TransferConsumer        │
  │ - topic, partitionId          │ ◇ aggregation
  │ + consumeFrom(startOffset)    │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a record ────────────────────────────────────

  [PRODUCED] → append → [AT OFFSET n] → [READ] → (seek) → [RE-READ]
  (records are immutable; only the read position moves)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────

  1. topic.produce("SAV2001", TXF-1)
  2.   → topic.partitionFor("SAV2001")  → 2
  3.   → partition[2].append(TXF-1)     → offset 0
  4. consumer.consumeFrom(0)
  5.   → partition[2].at(0), at(1), at(2)  in order
  6. consumer.consumeFrom(1)  (replay)

  Contract for append(record):
    Pre:  record non-null
    Post: record stored at the next offset; offset returned
    Guarantee: ordering preserved within this partition only
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
In Kafka, a topic, a partition, and an offset are three levels of the same storage model. A topic is a logical category of events, like a named folder — for example a transfers topic that holds all transfer events. A topic by itself stores nothing; it is split into one or more partitions, and partitions are where the data actually lives.

A partition is an ordered, append-only, immutable log stored on a broker. New records are always appended to the end and never changed. Kafka guarantees ordering only within a single partition, not across partitions, and partitions are the unit of parallelism — one partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in a group at a time. The record's partition is chosen by hashing its key, so the same key always lands in the same partition.

An offset is a sequential integer that identifies a record's position within one partition, starting at zero and increasing by one for each new record. Offsets are per-partition, and consumers commit the offset of the last record they processed so they can resume from exactly that point after a restart. To locate any record you need the triple of topic, partition, and offset.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, I key transfer events by account id so all of a customer's transfers land in the same partition and stay perfectly ordered, while different customers spread across partitions for parallel processing. Offsets let a crashed consumer resume exactly where it left off, and they let the fraud team seek back to an earlier offset to replay recent events after a model update, all without disturbing the other partitions. That is the elegance of the design — the topic gives you a clean category, the partition gives you ordering and parallelism, and the offset gives you precise position and replay.
